title: Least Squares
body:
Real data gives you $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ with more equations than unknowns and no solution
at all: 500 measurements, 3 parameters, and no line passes through 500 noisy points. **Least
squares is what you do instead of giving up.** If $\mathbf{b}$ is not in the column space of $A$,
find the $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ that gets as close as possible:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{x}} \|\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}\|_2
$$

## The geometric derivation

**This is the version worth knowing, and it is three sentences.** $A\mathbf{x}$ ranges over the
column space of $A$ as $\mathbf{x}$ varies, so the reachable set is a subspace. The closest point
of a subspace to $\mathbf{b}$ is its [[Projection]], by the best approximation theorem. Therefore
the residual $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ must be orthogonal to every column of
$A$:

$$
A^T(\mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \mathbf{0}
\;\iff\;
\boxed{A^TA\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^T\mathbf{b}}
$$

Those are the **normal equations**, and "normal" here means perpendicular, not typical. If $A$ has
independent columns then $A^TA$ is invertible and

$$
\hat{\mathbf{x}} = (A^TA)^{-1}A^T\mathbf{b}, \qquad A\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \underbrace{A(A^TA)^{-1}A^T}_{P}\mathbf{b}
$$

which is exactly the projection matrix from [[Projection]]. The two notes derive the same three
lines because they are the same problem: least squares *is* projection, with $\mathbf{b}$ renamed.

**No calculus was used.** The whole thing is one picture: drop a perpendicular onto a subspace.

## The statistical derivation, and why they agree

[[Linear Regression]] in [[STATISTICS]] arrives at the identical equations from the
other side. Regression minimises the sum of squared residuals

$$
\text{SSR} = \sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
$$

by setting the partial derivatives to zero. But $\text{SSR} = \|\mathbf{r}\|_2^2$, so **minimising
the sum of squares and projecting onto the column space are the same operation stated in two
languages.** The statistician's normal equations and the linear algebraist's orthogonality
condition are one equation, and the fitted values $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ are a projection of the
observed $\mathbf{y}$. That is the best pairing in the math block, and both courses should say so.

Two consequences that only the geometric view makes obvious:

- **The residual is orthogonal to every predictor.** So residuals correlated with a predictor mean
  your model is misspecified, not merely inaccurate. The geometry forbids it at the optimum.
- **$R^2$ is Pythagoras.** $\|\mathbf{y}_c\|^2 = \|\hat{\mathbf{y}}_c\|^2 + \|\mathbf{r}\|^2$ on
  centred data, and $R^2$ is the first term's share. Explained plus unexplained equals total
  because the two legs of a right triangle add to the hypotenuse.

Why *squared* residuals rather than absolute ones is a [[Vector Norm]] question: $L_2$ is the only
norm with an [[Inner Product]] behind it, so it is the only one where the answer is a projection
and comes in closed form. $L_1$ regression is more robust to outliers and has no formula like this.

## Fitting a line

To fit $y = c_0 + c_1x$ through points $(x_i, y_i)$, put the model in the columns:

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & x_1 \\ 1 & x_2 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_n \end{bmatrix},
\qquad \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} c_0 \\ c_1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ \vdots \\ y_n\end{bmatrix}
$$

**The model only has to be linear in the coefficients, not in $x$.** Columns of $x_i^2$, $\log
x_i$, or $\sin x_i$ fit parabolas, log curves, and harmonics with the same machinery. That is why
"linear regression" covers far more than straight lines, and it is the single most misread word in
the phrase.

## Computing it

| Method | Cost | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| Normal equations, $(A^TA)^{-1}A^T$ | cheapest | small, well-conditioned, by hand |
| [[Gram-Schmidt|QR]], $R\hat{\mathbf{x}} = Q^T\mathbf{b}$ | moderate | the default in practice |
| [[Singular Value Decomposition|SVD]], $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^+\mathbf{b}$ | dearest | rank deficient or badly conditioned |

**Do not form $A^TA$ if you can avoid it.** It squares the condition number, so a matrix you could
just about trust becomes one you cannot, and the same caution applies here as
[[Matrix Inverse]] gives about solving systems with an inverse. QR skips it entirely. When the
columns are dependent there is no unique $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ at all, and the [[Pseudoinverse]]
picks out the minimum-norm one.

## Related

- [[Projection]]: the same three lines
- [[Pseudoinverse]]: least squares written as one matrix
- [[Gram-Schmidt]]: how it is solved
- [[Vector Norm]] and [[Quadratic Form]]: why $L_2$, and why it is a minimum
- [[Linear Regression]] ([[STATISTICS]]): **the same equations derived by calculus**,
  plus residual plots, inference on the slope, and [[Correlation]]'s $r^2$
- [[Logistic Regression]] and [[Loss Function]]: the classification analogue, which swaps this
  loss for a probabilistic one and loses the closed form
